author: Carlos Martinez
title: USB Power Distribution and Peripheral Dropout: Why Your Wheel Cuts Out
description: Solve mid-race wheel, pedal, and button box disconnects by understanding USB power limits and hub architecture on your sim rig PC.

sections.p: A sudden loss of steering input during a race feels like a crash in real life. Your wheel goes dead, your pedals stop reporting inputs, your button box vanishes from device manager, and you're off the track before you even understand what happened. The problem is almost always not the wheel itself, but the USB power architecture feeding it. Most sim racers stack multiple high-current devices on a single hub or rely on passive hubs that have no power budget of their own. The result is brownout: not enough sustained power to keep all devices active, so the system disconnects and reconnects them to manage load.

Understanding USB power delivery and hub design prevents these drops completely. It requires knowing the difference between bus-powered and self-powered hubs, how much current your devices actually draw, and why daisy-chaining matters.

sections.h2: USB power limits and why passive hubs fail

sections.p: Every USB port on your PC has a maximum power budget. A standard USB 3.0 port can supply up to 900 mA (0.9 A) at 5V. A USB 2.0 port tops out at 500 mA. These are hard limits set by the USB standard, and once a device tries to draw more than the port can supply, the port shuts down the device to protect the motherboard.

A passive USB hub does not add power. It simply splits one port into four or seven ports, dividing that same 900 mA budget among all connected devices. If you plug a direct-drive wheelbase like a MOZA R9 (which can draw 400+ mA under load) plus a load cell pedal set (200+ mA) plus a button box (100+ mA) into a passive hub on a single port, you are asking one 900 mA port to supply over 700 mA to three devices before you even add a keyboard, mouse, or headset to the same hub. The port fails. Devices reconnect and disconnect in a loop, creating the random cutouts you experience mid-race.
Many budget hubs advertise "high-speed" or "USB 3.0" but supply zero external power. They rely entirely on the host port. This is the leading cause of peripheral dropout on sim racing rigs.

sections.h2: Self-powered hubs and external power supplies

sections.p: A self-powered hub has its own wall power supply, usually rated at 5V and 2A to 4A or higher. This hub pulls low current from the host PC port (just enough to signal and manage data) and supplies dedicated current from the wall to each of its downstream ports. Each port on a self-powered hub can then supply the full USB spec current, independent of the PC's port capacity.

For a sim rig, a self-powered hub is non-negotiable. Buy one rated for at least 2A total output and confirm it has an external power brick. Do not trust "powered" labels that show no wall adapter in the product photos. Check the specifications: look for "external power supply" and a wattage or amperage rating. A common reliable choice is a 7-port or 4-port hub with ~2A to 3A external supply and individual on/off switches per port. The switches let you manage power distribution and isolate devices that might be drawing excessive current.

list: Plug your MOZA R9 (or equivalent direct-drive wheel) into port 1 of a self-powered hub
Plug your load cell pedals into port 2
Plug your button box or shifter into port 3
Leave ports 4 and 5 free or use them for low-draw devices like a USB shift indicator or fan
Connect the hub's power adapter to a surge-protected power strip, not to your PC's USB power

sections.tip: A self-powered hub is cheap insurance. Expect to spend ~25 to 50 dollars for a reputable brand with a 2A or higher power supply. Skipping this step will cost you races.

sections.h2: Port saturation and the motherboard limit

sections.p: Even with a self-powered hub, the motherboard itself has limits. Most PC motherboards have a total USB power budget across all ports of around 2.0A per hub controller. Consumer boards typically have two controllers: one for USB 2.0 ports and one for USB 3.0. If you plug a self-powered hub into a USB 3.0 port and all its downstream devices are USB 3.0 devices, they can exceed the controller's ability to manage them, even though each port has its own power supply.

This is rare and usually only appears on heavily overloaded rigs with five or more high-current devices plus many low-current ones. The fix is to split your hub load across two separate self-powered hubs on two separate motherboard controllers (one on USB 2.0, one on USB 3.0, or one on each of two USB 3.0 headers).

sections.h2: Current draw: what your devices actually consume

sections.p: Understanding your device current draw helps you plan your hub layout and diagnose dropout causes. Direct-drive wheelbases vary widely. A MOZA R9 at mid-force (5 N.m of torque output) draws roughly 300 to 400 mA. At peak force (9 N.m), it may exceed 500 mA. Load cell pedals like the MOZA SR-P draw roughly 150 to 250 mA depending on how many axes are active. A USB button box or single-switch encoder draws 50 to 150 mA. A USB fan or LED strip draws 100 to 300 mA. A wireless headset receiver draws 100 to 200 mA.

Add these up. If your setup includes a MOZA R9 (500 mA at peak), MOZA SR-P pedals (250 mA), a button box (100 mA), and a USB fan (200 mA), you need at least 1050 mA of available current. A passive hub on a single 900 mA port will fail. A self-powered hub rated 2A (2000 mA) will handle this easily.

If you do not know your device's current draw, check the product manual or contact support. If a manual lists only voltage (5V) and watts, divide watts by 5 to get amps. A 2.5W device draws 2.5 / 5 = 0.5A or 500 mA.

Some sim racers try to extend a USB connection using passive extension cables or by plugging one hub into another hub. This can work if both hubs are self-powered, but it introduces unnecessary points of failure. A passive extension cable adds resistance and can degrade the signal, causing the device to draw more current to maintain a stable connection. A passive hub plugged into the downstream port of another hub does not gain any power advantage and may introduce signal integrity issues.

Use high-quality USB 3.0 cables rated for your device's requirements. If your direct-drive wheelbase came with a cable, use that cable. Do not substitute a cheaper or older USB 2.0 cable. Buy an extra self-powered hub if you need more ports rather than extending or daisy-chaining hubs.

If you are experiencing dropouts after setting up a self-powered hub, test your setup in Windows Device Manager. Open Device Manager, expand Universal Serial Bus controllers, and watch for devices with yellow warning icons during a sim race or FFB test. Yellow warnings indicate power or driver issues. Right-click and select Properties to see the error code.

If a device keeps disconnecting and reconnecting, disable USB selective suspend in Windows power settings. Open Control Panel, go to Power Options, click Change Plan Settings, then Change Advanced Power Settings, expand USB Settings, and set USB Selective Suspend to Off. This prevents Windows from power-cycling a USB device to save energy, which can mask (or cause) a real power delivery problem.

Also check your BIOS settings. Some motherboards allow you to adjust USB power delivery per port or per controller. If your BIOS has an option to disable USB power saving or to increase USB power delivery, enable it. These settings vary by manufacturer and model, so consult your motherboard manual.

olist: Open Device Manager and look for yellow warnings under Universal Serial Bus controllers
Disable USB Selective Suspend in Windows Power Options
Check your motherboard BIOS for USB power delivery settings and enable maximum power if available
Restart your PC and test during a practice session, not a race
If dropouts continue, try moving your hub to a different USB port on the motherboard (not the front panel)

sections.tip: Front-panel USB ports on many cases run through additional internal headers and can have higher resistance than rear motherboard ports. If your hub is on the front panel, move it to the rear I/O cluster and test again.

sections.p: Start with a quality self-powered hub rated for at least 2A of external power supply. Plug your high-current devices (wheelbase, pedals) into the first two ports. Leave a buffer of at least one empty port between high-current devices to avoid crosstalk. Plug low-current devices (button box, fan, indicator) into the remaining ports. If you have more than four high-current devices, buy a second self-powered hub and split the load. Connect both hubs to the rear USB ports of your motherboard on different headers if possible. This setup will eliminate USB power dropouts and keep your steering, pedals, and inputs responsive for every session.

faqs.q: Can I use a powered USB hub with just one high-current device?
faqs.a: Yes. If you only run a wheelbase and pedals, a single 2A self-powered hub will supply them reliably. The power overhead is small, but the stability gain is worth it. Dropout is binary: it either happens or it does not, and even one dropout during a race is unacceptable.

faqs.q: Does USB 3.0 give more power than USB 2.0?
faqs.a: USB 3.0 ports can supply the same 5V as USB 2.0, but the spec allows 900 mA per 3.0 port versus 500 mA per 2.0 port. However, this applies only to direct connections to the motherboard. A hub connected to any port receives power through the host port and relies on its own external supply for downstream ports. The hub's power rating is what matters, not whether it is USB 3.0 or 2.0.

faqs.q: Why does my wheel disconnect only during heavy FFB or long sessions?
faqs.a: During heavy FFB, your wheelbase draws peak current. If the total current demand from all USB devices on your hub exceeds the hub's rated supply, the hub controller shuts down. Long sessions cause heat to build up in the hub's power supply, which can reduce its effective output capacity. Both point to undersized or failing power delivery. Buy a hub rated for at least 1A more than your total device draw.

faqs.q: Is a laptop USB hub different from a desktop hub?
faqs.a: No fundamental difference, but laptop USB ports often have lower power budgets than desktop motherboard ports (some laptops limit USB to 500 mA per port). A self-powered hub is even more critical on a laptop. Buy one rated 2A or higher and confirm the external power adapter can supply that continuously without thermal cutoff.
